title: European Commission Proposes Quantum Act and New Sovereign Tech Equity Fund
html:
Insider Brief

  • The European Commission proposed a Quantum Act to commercialize European quantum research, strengthen supply chains and coordinate the transition to post-quantum cryptography.
  • The proposal would bring EU and national programs together to fund research, expand access to shared facilities and help companies bring quantum technologies to market.
  • The act would lay the groundwork for a Sovereign Tech Equity Fund to invest in strategic technologies, and the European Parliament and Council will now consider the proposal.

PRESS RELEASE — The European Commission today proposed the Quantum Act, a new framework to help turn Europe’s quantum research into products and services, strengthen supply chains and prepare Europe’s digital systems for post-quantum cryptography. The proposal also lays the groundwork for the Sovereign Tech Equity Fund (STEF).

The impact of quantum technologies will be profound, from navigation without satellites and faster drug discovery to ultra-advanced batteries and next-generation secure communications. Quantum technologies are moving from laboratories to products and services.

“Quantum technologies will shape the future of industry, security and innovation, and they will have a profound impact on our societies. Europe needs to accelerate now. With the Quantum Act, we are putting in place the key elements to turn our world-class quantum research into industrial capacity, strengthen critical supply chains and prepare for the cyber risks linked to quantum computing. Europe has already built strong foundations in quantum; now we must turn them into industrial scale, resilient supply chains and secure deployment. “– Henna Virkkunen, Executive Vice-President for Tech Sovereignty, Security and Democracy

The Quantum Act has three main pillars: research excellence, bringing quantum technology into use, and keeping systems and supplies secure. These will be delivered through the Quantum Europe Framework Initiative, which will bring together EU and national programmes around shared priorities for research and industry.

The Act will bring together European Union and national programmes around shared priorities for research, industry and deployment. It will improve access to financing, shared infrastructure and specialised support services. It will also support Europe’s transition to post-quantum cryptography, to help protect data, communications and critical infrastructure from future cyber risks linked to quantum computing.

Europe has strong research and promising companies, but it needs to scale up industrial capacity, market uptake and resilience in critical parts of the value chain. Alongside artificial intelligence, semiconductors and cloud, quantum is one of the critical technologies identified by the Commission.

Research and industrial deployment

The aim is to turn Europe’s strengths and leadership in quantum science into industrial capacity at scale.

The Commission also proposes Grand Challenges, targeted funding competitions and strategic initiatives designed to address major technological and engineering bottlenecks. Examples include building quantum computers that can keep working when errors occur and developing navigation devices that work without satellite signals.

The Act will also support the creation of pan-European quantum infrastructures for researchers and companies across Europe. These include quantum computers, quantum simulators and quantum-enhanced medical imaging. Quantum Technology and Innovation Hubs will provide specialised knowledge, engineering expertise and skills to help start-ups and small and medium-sized enterprises develop market-ready products.

The EU and Member States will also focus on strategic projects to scale up key quantum capabilities, including industrial applications and manufacturing. The Act will also help companies access financing and connect with public buyers.

Security, supply chains and finance

Quantum technologies are increasingly important for security, with both civilian and dual-use applications. The Commission and Member States will work together to monitor supply chains, identify critical suppliers and components, and reduce supply-chain risks.

The EU will also work with international partners to strengthen supply chains and protect shared security interests. The Act will support a coordinated transition to post-quantum cryptography, with preparedness monitoring and targeted procurement safeguards to help keep Europe’s digital systems secure.

The Act also allows for the establishment of a new investment vehicle: the Sovereign Tech Equity Fund. It will provide equity and similar types of financing to support technologies that are essential for the Union’s technological sovereignty and economic security. It will help fund the Quantum Europe Framework Initiative and the measures outlined in the Commission’s Tech Sovereignty Package.

Putting the Quantum Act into practice

A Quantum Strategy Board will bring together the Commission and Member States to ensure strategic coordination of national and European programmes. A European Quantum Alliance will bring together private and public stakeholders, including supply and demand companies, universities, research and technology organisations, to support this effort.

The European High-Performance Computing Joint Undertaking, or its successor, would be the main body carrying out EU-level quantum research, innovation and infrastructure work.

The Commission will also work closely with the European Investment Bank Group, the Member States and other key stakeholders to swiftly establish the Sovereign Tech Equity Fund for the financial support of technologies that are essential for the Union’s technological sovereignty and economic security.

Next steps

The European Parliament and the Council will now consider the proposal.

Background

The proposal supports the Quantum Europe Strategy’s goal of making Europe a global leader in quantum technologies by 2030. Future EU funding under the Quantum Act would depend on budget decisions and the rules of the programmes concerned.

The 2025 Quantum Europe Strategy reported more than €11 billion in public quantum investment by the EU and its Member States. This includes support for research through the Quantum Flagship, secure communications networks and a European network of quantum computers.

MENTIONED IN THE ARTICLE

The Commission represents and upholds the interests of the EU as a whole, and is independent of national governments. The European Commission prepares legislation for adoption by the Council (representing the member countries) and the Parliament (representing the citizens). It administers the budget and the policy programmes (agriculture, fisheries, research etc.) in cooperation with authorities in the member countries.
